extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, policymakers, and the general public interested in liberty and limits of social authority
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and principles for when society may legitimately interfere with an individual's actions, plus principles defending individuality, diversity, eccentricity, and the social value of genius. Distinguishes self-regarding from other-regarding conduct and prescribes appropriate social/legal responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of individuality as development
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuality is the same thing with development; the cultivation of individuality produces well-developed human beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that human faculties were given to be 'cultivated and unfolded, not rooted out and consumed' and that as each person's individuality develops, 'each person becomes more valuable to himself, and is therefore capable of being more valuable to others.' This functions as a normative criterion for favoring freedom and diversity of life-plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom for self-regarding actions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person's conduct 'affects the interests of no persons besides himself, or needs not affect them unless they like (all the persons concerned being of full age, and the ordinary amount of understanding)', there should be 'perfect freedom, legal and social, to do the action and stand the consequences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a clear rule: adults of ordinary understanding should have legal and social liberty over matters that concern only themselves. Interference in these cases is illegitimate because others' general presumptions are likely misapplied to individual circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal authority when actions harm others
rubrics_metrics.description: 'As soon as any part of a person's conduct affects prejudicially the interests of others, society has jurisdiction over it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society may intervene when an action prejudicially affects others' interests; the central test for legitimate interference is whether the conduct harms others (i.e., infringes interests/rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement of non-injury and civic obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Society is justified in enforcing conduct consisting first in not injuring the interests of one another and secondly in each person's bearing his share (fixed on an equitable principle) of the labours and sacrifices incurred for defending the society or its members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These obligations 'society is justified in enforcing, at all costs to those who endeavour to withhold fulfilment.' This distinguishes duties society can coerce (non-injury, fair contribution to defenses) from purely self-regarding choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social censure for harmful but non-rights-violating acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts may be hurtful to others or wanting in due consideration without violating constituted rights; 'the offender may then be justly punished by opinion though not by law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where conduct is improper but not legally wrongful, society may legitimately apply moral disapproval and social consequences rather than legal punishment; the distinction between legal coercion and social sanction is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference must rest on general presumptions and is fallible
rubrics_metrics.description: The interference of society to overrule a person's judgment in matters that only concern him 'must be grounded on general presumptions; which may be altogether wrong, and even if right, are as likely as not to be misapplied to individual cases.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cautions against paternalistic coercion: general presumptions about what is good for people are an unreliable basis for overruling individual choices, because outsiders lack specific knowledge of the individual's circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use persuasion, not coercion, for self-regarding virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinterested benevolence should persuade and educate rather than coerce; 'education works by conviction and persuasion as well as by compulsion, and it is by the former only that, when the period of education is past, the self-regarding virtues should be inculcated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society may exhort, advise, or attempt to persuade adults about their own good, but coercive measures (laws, force) are inappropriate for purely self-regarding matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of the individual's judgment about his own good
rubrics_metrics.description: 'He himself is the final judge' of what concerns his own feelings and circumstances; others' interest in his well-being is 'fractional, and altogether indirect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the individual has superior access to his own feelings and circumstances, society should defer to individual judgment except in cases where others' interests are implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of eccentricity and nonconformity
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere example of nonconformity and 'the mere refusal to bend the knee to custom, is itself a service'; eccentricity is desirable as a corrective to the 'tyranny of opinion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society should tolerate eccentricity because it breaks conformity and can lead to improvements; penalizing or stigmatizing nonconformity undermines the social benefit of originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of genius by an atmosphere of freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Genius can only breathe freely in an atmosphere of freedom' — exceptional individuals need scope to act differently from the mass if they are to initiate improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public policy and social attitudes should preserve conditions in which original, creative, or genius individuals can experiment and act without undue compression into social moulds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for diversity of modes of life
rubrics_metrics.description: Different persons 'require different conditions for their spiritual development' and 'the same mode of life is a healthy excitement to one... while to another it is a distracting burden.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolerance for a plurality of ways of living is justified because one uniform pattern of life will not suit all natures; public sentiment should allow people to 'lead different lives' within limits that protect others' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to the despotism of custom
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Whatever crushes individuality is despotism, by whatever name it may be called' and the 'despotism of custom is everywhere the standing hindrance to human advancement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social and political institutions should resist mechanisms (custom, public opinion, organised pressures) that enforce uniformity and thereby stifle progress; plurality of paths fosters improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: treating nonconformity as insanity/legal incapacitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning against practices that 'lay before the jury as evidence of insanity' any appearance unlike absolute commonplace, and thereby judicially declare eccentric persons unfit for management of their affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill critiques the tendency to use legal processes (committal, guardianship) to punish or dispossess people for eccentricity — an abuse of social power that violates the legitimate limits of authority over individuals.
